newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo '97 wheat buy up seen below plan, analysts.
newsitem.headline: Yugo '97 wheat buy up seen below plan, analysts.

text.p: Yugoslavia will fail to buy up planned quantities of 1997 wheat crop from its farmers because of unfavourable payment conditions, analysts said on Thursday.

The government's plan is to buy up to one million tonnes of this year's wheat crop. It has already purchased some 350,000 tonnes of wheat in advance and intends to buy another 600,000 tonnes after the harvest.
Analysts doubt farmers will sell all of their crop immediately. Many will store it and sell it when they want.

"It can be expected that the farmers sell only a minimum of their wheat crop just to get enough money to cover sowing costs," undersecretary in the federal Agriculture Ministry Milan Prostran told Reuters.
Official preliminary 1997 wheat forecasts stand at 2.8 million tonnes from some 800,000 hectares against 1.5 million tonnes from 583,000 ha harvested in 1996.
The country's annual needs are estimated between two and 2.4 million tonnes.
Past few days of heavy rainfalls and hail damaged huge wheat areas in the country's granary Vojvodina and analysts said the crop could be a few percent below the official forecast.
Shortages last year pushed price of wheat up to 1.4 or at some points even 1.7 dinars per kilo compared to the guaranteed price of 0.9 dinars for '96 crop.

Farmers who sold their wheat in winter months earned more than those who sold their crop to the state immediately after harvest which will have a psychological effect on the sale of wheat to the state this year, analysts said.
The Serbian government set the purchasing price of this year's crop at 1.1 dinar per kilo.

Forty percent of the total value will be paid in cash by the end of August. The second and third instalments of 30 percent each will be paid in forward wheat contracts issued by Serbia's Commodity Reserve Agency maturing end of September and end of October.
Wheat can also be exchanged for fuel, fertilisers, seeds and agricultural equipment.
Agricultural producers saw the purchasing price as satisfactory, but were not happy with delayed payments.
"The price is good and farmers are happy with it. But payouts are late. Farmers demand to be paid in time," said Milan Pavlovic of the Association of Agricultural Cooperatives of Serbia.
"The farmers must buy fertilisers, seeds, prepare for next sowing. If the government wants them to invest in production they must get money on time," he said.
Analysts worried that 1996 would repeat itself when the government had no money to pay farmers for their crops.

"Vojvodina farmers are still owed some 100 million dinars ($17.23 million) for the '96 crop. Final payment is set for end of October and that is too late as it is already time of sowing," said Ljiljana Vasic, head of the Association of Agricultural Cooperatives of Vojvodina.

"At least 50-60 percent should be paid in cash. Money received for wheat is this year's first payment for crops to farmers who need it for re-investment and to prepare their children for school," she said. -- Belgrade Newsroom +381 11 311 4254
